title: Committee for Public Counsel Services v. Middlesex and Suffolk County District Courts
description: Whether State court judges are authorized to increase compensation rates for bar advocates above levels set by the Legislature, with the plaintiff arguing for judicial authority to increase rates and the defendant arguing against it due to separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The Committee for Public Counsel Services (CPCS) contended that the court should order increased compensation rates for bar advocates due to a recent shortage of counsel for indigent criminal defendants.
defendant_argument: The Middlesex and Suffolk County District Courts and the intervener (Boston Municipal Court and district attorney for the Suffolk district) opposed judicially ordered compensation rates, arguing that such an order would violate the separation of powers doctrine.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petitioner's request for judicially ordered increased compensation rates for bar advocates, concluding that the Legislature's actions and existing protocols were sufficient to address the counsel shortage and that extraordinary circumstances justifying judicial intervention were not demonstrated.

title: Commonwealth v. Arias
description: Whether a 24-hour delay in conducting a motor vehicle stop after observing a civil traffic infraction is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment and art. 14 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the delay was reasonable because the officer could not safely stop the defendant at the time of the infraction and did not maintain immediate surveillance.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the 24-hour delay was unreasonable, violating constitutional protections against unreasonable searches and seizures, especially given the pretextual nature of the stop.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's denial of the defendant's motion to suppress, vacated the conviction, and remanded the case, finding the 24-hour delayed traffic stop unreasonable.

title: Tran v. Commonwealth
description: Whether a former State senator is immune from criminal prosecution for misusing public resources for reelection campaigns under legislative immunity and separation of powers principles, and whether the grand jury process was impaired by the prosecutor's exclusion of a grand juror.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the defendant's actions were not protected by legislative immunity or separation of powers, and that the grand jury process was not impaired.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued he was immune from prosecution under legislative immunity (Art. 21) and separation of powers (Arts. 10 and 11) for using staff for campaign activities, and that the prosecutor's exclusion of a grand juror impaired the grand jury proceedings.
decision_outcome: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, ruling that he is not immune from prosecution and that the grand jury proceedings were not impaired to warrant dismissal.

title: Raftery v. State Board of Retirement
description: Whether the mandatory forfeiture of a public employee's pension benefits, following a criminal conviction related to their office, constitutes an excessive fine or cruel and unusual punishment under Article 26 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the total forfeiture of his pension and health insurance benefits, as mandated by law, violated Article 26's prohibitions against excessive fines and cruel or unusual punishment, asserting Article 26 provides greater protection than the Eighth Amendment.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State Board of Retirement, argued that the pension forfeiture was a lawful consequence of the plaintiff's criminal conviction involving his office and did not constitute an excessive fine or cruel and unusual punishment under Article 26.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the retirement board's decision, ruling that the pension forfeiture does not violate Article 26's excessive fines or cruel and unusual punishment provisions.

title: Care and Prevention of Eve
description: Whether the Department of Children and Families (DCF) can vaccinate a child in its temporary custody against the religious objections of the parents, with parents arguing against vaccination based on religious freedom and DCF arguing for vaccination based on the child's best interest and public health.
plaintiff_argument: The parents, practicing Rastafarians, argued that vaccinating their child over their sincerely held religious objections, while they only temporarily lost custody, violates their constitutional rights to direct their child's religious upbringing, especially given existing state religious exemptions and DCF's inconsistent application of vaccination requirements.
defendant_argument: The Department of Children and Families (DCF) and the child's counsel argued that vaccinations are medically necessary for the child's best interest and public health, and that their authority includes routine medical care for children in their custody. They contended that the parents' objections should be balanced against the child's interests and the Commonwealth's interest in keeping all children safe.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's order, ruling that the Department of Children and Families failed to demonstrate that allowing the child to remain unvaccinated would substantially hinder the state's compelling public health interests, thereby upholding the parents' religious freedom rights.

title: Commonwealth v. Govan
description: Whether the initial imposition of GPS monitoring as a condition of pretrial release constitutes a constitutional search under art. 14 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, and whether the subsequent warrantless retrieval and review of GPS location data for a criminal investigation is also a search under art. 14.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the initial GPS monitoring was a constitutional search due to the defendant's consent and legitimate governmental interests, and that the subsequent data retrieval was not a search under art. 14.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that both the initial imposition of GPS monitoring and the subsequent retrieval of location data constituted unconstitutional searches under art. 14.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the motion judge's order denying the defendant's motion to suppress, ruling that the initial imposition of GPS monitoring was a reasonable and constitutional search, and the subsequent retrieval and review of GPS location data was not a search under art. 14.

title: Commonwealth v. Dilworth
description: Whether a Superior Court judge abused discretion in dismissing indictments with prejudice as a sanction for the Commonwealth's refusal to comply with a discovery order, which was sought by the defendant to challenge alleged discriminatory social media monitoring practices on equal protection grounds.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the dismissal was an inappropriate sanction, the judge applied the wrong legal standard for equal protection discovery, and the requested information (undercover Snapchat usernames and profile images) was privileged, thus shielding it from disclosure.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the discovery was relevant and material to challenge a discriminatory investigatory practice on equal protection grounds, and that the Commonwealth's deliberate refusal to produce court-ordered discovery warranted dismissal.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Judicial Court affirmed the Superior Court judge's decision to dismiss the indictments with prejudice, finding no abuse of discretion.

title: Commonwealth v. Hastings
description: Whether the constitutionally mandated exception to the indigency statute, carved out in Diatchenko II, authorizes a judge to allow an indigent prisoner's motion for funds to retain an expert witness for an upcoming parole hearing.
plaintiff_argument: Hastings argued that the indigency statute's exception, which allows funds for expert witnesses, should apply to his case to fund a social services advocate for his parole hearing, as it implicates his constitutional right to reasonable disability accommodations.
defendant_argument: The motion judge argued that the indigency statute only applies to pending court proceedings and appeals, and the Diatchenko II exception does not extend to statutory parole hearings, which arise by statute, not constitutional mandate.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the lower court's decision, ruling that the constitutionally mandated exception to the indigency statute applies, authorizing funds for a social services advocate for Hastings's parole hearing.

title: Commonwealth v. Shepherd
description: Whether the abolition of felony-murder as an independent theory of liability should apply retroactively to the defendant's case, given claims of equal protection violations due to racial disparities in its application.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argues that the decision in Brown to abolish felony-murder as an independent theory of liability should apply only prospectively, as previously determined and reaffirmed, and that this prospective application does not violate equal protection principles because it was a neutral decision without discriminatory purpose and does not burden a fundamental right.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the decision in Brown should apply retroactively to his case because the prospective application violates equal protection principles, citing data showing racial disparities in felony-murder convictions that disproportionately affect Black persons.
decision_outcome: The defendant's conviction of murder in the first degree is affirmed, and the orders denying his motions for a new trial are also affirmed.

title: Six Brothers, Inc. v. Town of Brookline
description: Whether the town of Brookline's bylaw, which incrementally prohibits tobacco sales based on birth year, is preempted by the state Tobacco Act or violates the State Constitution's equal protection provisions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff retailers argued that the bylaw is preempted by the state Tobacco Act because it sets a different minimum sales age standard, and it violates the State Constitution's equal protection provisions by discriminating based on birth year.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the Town of Brookline, argued that the bylaw is not preempted by the state Tobacco Act as it augments, rather than conflicts with, the state's minimum age standard, and it is rationally related to the legitimate government interest of public health, thus not violating equal protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the dismissal of the retailers' complaint, ruling that the bylaw is not preempted by the state Tobacco Act and does not violate the State Constitution's equal protection provisions.

title: Graham v. District Attorney for Hampden District
description: Whether the District Attorney's office failed to comply with its obligations to disclose and investigate evidence of police misconduct, with plaintiffs arguing they failed and the defendant arguing they fulfilled their duties.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argue that the district attorney's office failed to adequately investigate and disclose evidence of police misconduct, requesting court-ordered remedies including a list of implicated officers and a presumption favoring the DOJ report.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that its office has fulfilled its obligations to disclose and investigate police misconduct, asserting that all relevant information is known and that extensive efforts have been made to obtain and disclose DOJ-reviewed materials.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the district attorney's office breached its duties to disclose and investigate police misconduct, ordering it to obtain and disclose all relevant documents reviewed by the DOJ to the plaintiffs.

title: Commonwealth v. Mattis
description: Whether mandatory life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for emerging adults (18-20 years old) violates Article 26 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that a mandatory life sentence without parole for emerging adults is constitutional if imposed after an individualized hearing.
defendant_argument: Sheldon Mattis argued that it is unconstitutional to sentence an emerging adult to life without the possibility of parole in any circumstance.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that mandatory life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for emerging adults (18-20 years old) is unconstitutional under Article 26 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights and remanded the case for resentencing.

title: Commonwealth v. Rader
description: Whether the police stop and frisk of the defendant violated his Fourth Amendment rights due to a lack of reasonable suspicion or his equal protection rights due to racial profiling.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the police stop was lawful, based on reasonable suspicion, and that the officers had a race-neutral reason for the stop, rebutting any inference of discriminatory motive.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the stop lacked reasonable suspicion and violated his equal protection rights due to racial profiling, supported by statistical evidence of discriminatory policing.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of the defendant's motion to suppress, concluding that the stop did not violate his Fourth Amendment or equal protection rights.

title: Commonwealth v. Privette
description: Whether, under the collective knowledge doctrine, information known to other investigating officers may be imputed to the officer who initiated a stop to establish reasonable suspicion without violating Article 14 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The investigatory stop was constitutionally permissible, and Dwan's knowledge (including the suspect having facial hair) should be imputed to Doherty under the horizontal collective knowledge doctrine to establish reasonable suspicion.
defendant_argument: The investigatory stop was unconstitutional because the acting officer lacked reasonable suspicion, and the horizontal collective knowledge doctrine should not be applied, or at least not broadly enough to impute Dwan's and Lopez's knowledge to Doherty.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of the defendant's motion to suppress evidence, finding that the investigatory stop was constitutionally permissible based on reasonable suspicion, with Dwan's knowledge imputed to Doherty under a limited horizontal collective knowledge doctrine.

title: Barron v. Kolenda
description: Whether a town's public comment policy, which includes civility restraints on the content of speech, violates the rights to assemble and speak in a peaceable manner and to free speech under Articles 19 and 16 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The town's public comment policy is unconstitutional because it disallows criticism of board members and their decisions and regulates protected speech based on content and viewpoint, violating state constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: The town's public comment policy is constitutional and necessary to maintain an orderly and peaceable public comment session at governmental meetings.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Judicial Court reversed the Superior Court's judgment, declaring the town's public comment policy unconstitutional under Articles 19 and 16 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Kligler v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights provides a substantive due process right to physician-assisted suicide, which the plaintiffs argue it does, and the defendants argue it does not and is prohibited by law.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that terminally ill patients with six months or less to live have a constitutional right to receive a prescription for lethal medication to bring about death at a time and in a manner of their choosing, and that physicians should not be prosecuted for providing such assistance.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that physician-assisted suicide is not immune from prosecution in Massachusetts, that the law of manslaughter may prohibit it without offending constitutional protections, and that there is no fundamental right to physician-assisted suicide.
decision_outcome: The court concluded that the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights does not protect physician-assisted suicide and that the law of manslaughter may prohibit it without offending constitutional protections. Kligler's claim was dismissed for lack of an actual controversy, while the Superior Court's summary judgment order against Steinbach was affirmed.

title: Welter v. Board of Registration in Medicine
description: Whether due process requires the Board of Registration in Medicine to prove common-law fraud elements, such as intent and reliance, before suspending a physician's license for deceptive advertising or conduct.
plaintiff_argument: Dr. Welter argued that his due process rights were violated because the board suspended his license without proving common-law fraud elements like intent and patient reliance, and that the sanction was excessive.
defendant_argument: The Board of Registration in Medicine argued that its regulations do not require proof of common-law fraud elements, are rationally related to protecting public health and confidence, and its decision and sanction were appropriate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Judicial Court affirmed the Board of Registration in Medicine's decision, ruling that the regulations do not violate due process and the board's findings and sanction were supported by evidence.

title: Rodriguez v. Massachusetts Parole Board
description: Whether the Massachusetts Parole Board's denial of parole to a juvenile offender sentenced to life in prison denied him the "meaningful opportunity to obtain release" guaranteed by the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the parole board's fourth denial of his parole request denied him the "meaningful opportunity to obtain release" afforded to juvenile offenders sentenced to life in prison, despite his rehabilitative efforts and advanced age.
defendant_argument: The Massachusetts Parole Board argued that its decision was consistent with the law, that the plaintiff was "not yet rehabilitated," and his release was "not compatible with the welfare of society," after properly considering youth-related factors.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts affirmed the Superior Court's judgment, which upheld the parole board's decision to deny the plaintiff release on parole.

title: Lyons v. Secretary of the Commonwealth
description: Whether the Massachusetts Legislature has the constitutional authority to enact universal early voting provisions and other election reforms under the VOTES act, or if these provisions are unconstitutional under Article 45 and other parts of the Massachusetts Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the universal early voting provisions of the VOTES act are facially unconstitutional because Article 45 of the Massachusetts Constitution limits voting to in-person on election day, except for specific absentee voting circumstances. They also challenged poll worker appointment rules, electioneering bans, electronic voting for disabled/overseas voters, and counting ballots of voters who die after casting.
defendant_argument: The Secretary of the Commonwealth argued that the Legislature has broad constitutional powers to regulate elections and enhance voting opportunities, and that the VOTES act's provisions are consistent with the Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled in favor of the Secretary of the Commonwealth on all claims, denying the plaintiffs' request for injunctive relief and upholding the constitutionality of the VOTES act.

title: Anderson v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Attorney General's summary and the 'yes' and 'no' statements for a legislative amendment proposing a graduated income tax are unfair and misleading, with plaintiffs arguing they are and defendants arguing they are not.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs contend that the summary and 'yes' and 'no' statements mislead voters by suggesting additional tax revenue would increase education and transportation spending, when the Legislature could potentially redirect existing funds.
defendant_argument: The defendants argue that the summary and statements are fair, concise, and accurately track the language of the proposed amendment, and are not required to include legal analysis of potential flaws or how the Legislature might spend other monies.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Attorney General's summary and the 'yes' and 'no' statements comply with constitutional and statutory requirements, disagreeing with the plaintiffs' claims of unfairness and misleading content.

title: Koussa v. Attorney General
description: Whether the Attorney General's certification of initiative petitions, which define app-based drivers as independent contractors and limit network companies' tort liability, violates the related subjects requirement of the Massachusetts Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the initiative petitions contained two substantively distinct policy decisions, violating the related subjects requirement of art. 48, and that the Attorney General's summaries of the proposed laws were unfair.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General argued that the petitions complied with art. 48, containing only related subjects, and that the summaries were fair. Interveners contended that the tort liability provisions were merely downstream consequences of defining the driver-company relationship.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Attorney General's certifications of the initiative petitions were in error because the petitions violated the related subjects requirement of art. 48, and therefore the petitions cannot be placed on the ballot.

title: Colpack v. Attorney General
description: Whether Initiative Petition 21-03 meets the "related subjects" requirement of art. 48 of the Massachusetts Constitution for ballot initiatives, which mandates that a petition contain only subjects that are related or mutually dependent.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Attorney General's certification was improper because Initiative Petition 21-03 does not meet the related subjects requirement, as its provisions are substantively distinct, combine contradictory positions, and its risk mitigation measures are ill-suited or ineffective.
defendant_argument: The Attorney General contended that Initiative Petition 21-03 was properly certified because its various provisions form an integrated scheme, sharing a common purpose of modernizing alcohol sales and mitigating potential negative effects, thus satisfying the related subjects requirement.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Attorney General's certification of Initiative Petition 21-03, concluding that the petition is in proper form to be submitted to the voters.

title: Commonwealth v. Sweeting-Bailey
description: Whether police officers had reasonable suspicion to pat frisk the defendant, a passenger in a vehicle stopped for a traffic violation, based on the erratic behavior of another passenger and other factors.
plaintiff_argument: The officers had reasonable suspicion based on the totality of circumstances, including a companion's distracting behavior, the occupants' criminal histories involving firearms, and gang affiliations, to believe the defendant was armed and dangerous.
defendant_argument: The officers' suspicion was a "mere hunch" not supported by objectively reasonable facts, as the defendant himself was cooperative, and the other factors were insufficient to justify the patfrisk.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the denial of the defendant's motion to suppress, ruling that the patfrisk was constitutional.

title: Commonwealth v. Dejesus
description: Whether the evidence obtained from a warrantless search should be suppressed because the defendant lacked a reasonable expectation of privacy in the searched area, and whether the separate standing requirement under Article 14 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights should be abolished.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that the motion to suppress was properly denied because the defendant did not have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the basement, and there was sufficient evidence to prove possession of the firearm.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the firearm and feeding device should have been suppressed as fruits of a warrantless search because he lacked a reasonable expectation of privacy in the basement, and that there was insufficient evidence that he possessed the firearm.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the defendant's convictions for possessing a firearm without a license and a large capacity feeding device, denying the motion to suppress and abolishing the separate standing requirement under Article 14.

title: Edwards v. Commonwealth
description: Whether the Massachusetts whistleblower act applies to the dismissal of the Sex Offender Registry Board (SORB) chair by the Governor, and whether genuine issues of material fact remain regarding the plaintiff's claim of retaliatory termination.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that her dismissal as SORB chair was a retaliatory action under the Massachusetts whistleblower act because she objected to a legally erroneous decision by a hearing examiner, which she reasonably believed violated a law or policy.
defendant_argument: The Commonwealth argues that the whistleblower act does not apply to the Governor's dismissal of the SORB chair, that the Governor's actions are not attributable to the Commonwealth, that the act conflicts with the registration act (which states the chair serves "at the pleasure of the governor"), and that its application violates the constitutional principle of separation of powers.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's denial of the Commonwealth's motion for summary judgment, concluding that the whistleblower act is applicable in these circumstances and that genuine issues of material fact remain in dispute, allowing the case to proceed.

title: Commonwealth v. Delgado-Rivera
description: Whether Jorge Delgado-Rivera had a reasonable expectation of privacy in text messages he sent that were stored on another person's cellular telephone, with Delgado-Rivera arguing he had such an interest and the Commonwealth arguing he did not.
plaintiff_argument: The Commonwealth argued that Delgado-Rivera had no standing to challenge the search of the cellular telephone because he had no reasonable expectation of privacy in the text messages stored on another person's device.
defendant_argument: Delgado-Rivera argued that he had a privacy interest in the text messages he sent that were stored on his codefendant's cellular telephone and therefore had standing to challenge the search.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Delgado-Rivera had no reasonable expectation of privacy in the text messages sent by him and stored on another person's cellular telephone, vacating the lower court's decision to allow his motion to suppress.
